intro: The cor anglais melody became “Goin’ Home” only after Dvořák’s death. Around that apparently simple song he builds a slow movement with a minor-key middle, a sudden orchestral confrontation and a retreat into chamber music.
question: How does a song change when the orchestra surrounds it?

sections.label: Song returns · approximate
sections.mNote: song returns quietly, with later strings reduced towards chamber scale

sections.label: Closing chords · approximate

relations.label: The cor anglais song returns
relations.basis: The large A–B–A′ design restores the opening song after the central minor-key and climactic passages. The later excerpt begins at the return marked near 520 s, not at an inferred instrument entrance. CENS diagonal mean 0.927, sustained 27.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 482.5 s (cache/form/dvorak-9-largo.txt, candidate 2; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Chords before the song
cues.text: The opening contrasts a sequence of chords with the long melody that follows. Keep both shapes in mind: the introduction is not merely a count-in, and its chordal writing will matter again near the close.
cues.evidence: The Antonín Dvořák work guide describes the introductory chords and their later return. This identifies the opening design, not a precisely timed instrumental entrance. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A melody with few pitches
cues.text: In the opening song, listen for the tune’s limited collection of pitches and long breaths. The cor anglais is the melody’s principal instrument in the score; focus on the line rather than waiting for a new orchestral event.
cues.evidence: The work guide documents the cor anglais melody and its pentatonic character. Its broad location follows the quieter passage after about 0:24, not an aurally verified entrance. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Written in New York
cues.text: Dvořák composed the symphony in New York between 10 January and 24 May 1893. It belongs to the first year of his American appointment; the score was complete before his summer in Spillville, Iowa.
cues.evidence: The Antonín Dvořák work catalogue gives the composition dates and explains that the symphony preceded the inland summer visit. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

cues.title: A swell and a withdrawal
cues.text: Across this stretch, the quiet writing expands into a stronger passage before dropping back. Keep following the phrase through the change in weight rather than treating the crest as a new beginning.
cues.evidence: The report shows rising relative level around 2:10–2:25 followed by a marked reduction around 2:30. It does not identify which players produce the change.

cues.title: “Goin’ Home” came later
cues.text: William Arms Fisher, one of Dvořák’s American pupils, made “Goin’ Home” from the Largo melody in 1922. The song followed the symphony, not the other way round.
cues.evidence: The work guide’s performance-history section dates Fisher’s vocal arrangement and quotes his account of making it. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

cues.title: Support beneath the melody
cues.text: Through the quieter continuation, attend to the accompaniment as well as the tune. Sustained support can change the harmony without producing a conspicuous new attack.
cues.evidence: The report finds relatively few attacks around 3:05–3:50. The distinction between melody and support is a listening invitation, not a machine identification of separate parts.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A contrasting middle
cues.text: The middle section turns towards C♯ minor, contrasting with the song’s D♭ major. Those tonic names refer to the same piano key; the surrounding notes change the harmonic setting.
cues.evidence: The work guide documents the minor-key middle. Increased activity near 4:30 and the following pitch estimates support its approximate location; they do not provide a score alignment. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two rates of movement
cues.text: Through the middle section, distinguish small moving figures from the longer span of the phrase. The accompaniment need not follow every melodic note for the music to maintain its direction.
cues.evidence: This is a passage-level listening suggestion for the documented contrasting middle. The analysis cannot separate its instrumental lines.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The texture draws inward
cues.text: In this stretch, the sound retreats and the attacks become more widely spaced. Listen through that withdrawal: reduced activity need not signal a return to the opening melody.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls around 6:10–6:35, with few attacks detected around 6:35–6:40. The report supports a textural retreat, not a theme identification.

cues.title: Harry Burleigh’s singing
cues.text: Harry T. Burleigh sang spirituals for Dvořák in New York. Dvořák distinguished writing in the spirit of such melodies from inserting existing tunes: he made that distinction both in interviews and in correspondence.
cues.evidence: The work guide discusses Burleigh and quotes Dvořák’s statements to the New York Herald and to Oskar Nedbal. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

cues.title: The surface gathers motion
cues.text: Across this passage, closely packed activity grows out of the preceding stillness. Follow both the smaller notes and the increase in weight as the movement approaches its central crest.
cues.evidence: Attack density increases around 7:45–7:55, and relative level rises through approximately 8:00–8:15.

cues.title: A crest within the symphony
cues.text: The Largo’s central climax combines its own material with themes from the first movement. Listen for the contrast between a single singing line and several ideas sharing a larger orchestral statement.
cues.evidence: The work guide documents the combined themes. The recording’s strongest region around 8:10–8:20 suggests its broad location; no individual theme entrance is verified. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A smaller scale again
cues.text: In the later return, compare the song’s quieter scale with the preceding orchestral weight. A familiar phrase can feel more exposed after the surrounding texture has receded.
cues.evidence: The guide describes the quiet thematic return. The low-level stretch after about 8:40 is consistent with that position, but the melody is not independently identified by the report.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Do not fill the gaps
cues.text: Through the late quiet phrases, attend to the spaces and remaining resonance. A phrase can continue through a held sound without requiring another attack to keep its shape.
cues.evidence: The analysis shows few detected attacks and comparatively low relative level across much of 9:00–9:45. It does not distinguish every rest from a sustained note.

cues.title: Carnegie Hall, December 1893
cues.text: Anton Seidl conducted the New York Philharmonic in the premiere on 16 December 1893. A public rehearsal had taken place the previous afternoon; these are dates for the work’s first performances, not for this recording.
cues.evidence: The work catalogue and its premiere account distinguish the public rehearsal on 15 December from the concert on 16 December. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

cues.title: The frame returns
cues.text: Near the close, the introductory chordal writing returns before the final withdrawal. Compare the pacing of those chords with the song’s melodic breathing; both have helped organise the movement.
cues.evidence: The return of the introductory chords is documented in the work guide. Their placement is approximate: the recording changes around 10:40–11:04 and then recedes. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The bass settles beneath one voice
transitions.how: The introductory wind chords travel from E major into the distant D♭ region. Their last move, G♭ minor to D♭ major, is a minor-subdominant plagal cadence: G♭ falls to F while the bass settles on D♭. The chordal ensemble then withdraws, leaving the cor anglais over muted strings. Instead of the introduction’s chromatic shifts, the tune begins with a small pentatonic collection and long breaths. Harmony establishes the new ground first; a single reed voice then makes it sound inhabitable.
transitions.evidence: Section boundary: Opening song, 24 s. The report marks 0:24 and falls to −30.9 dB at 0:25 from −10.7 dB at 0:15. The Dvořák work guide prints the introductory chord succession and identifies cor anglais with muted strings; the score supplies the voice-leading. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

transitions.title: The tonic stays, its mode changes
transitions.how: After the D♭ major song subsides, Dvořák keeps the same sounding tonic but respells it C♯ and turns to minor. E♮ replaces the major third F: the harmonic change is close under the fingers even though the notation acquires sharps. More mobile wind phrases and string figures replace the cor anglais melody’s broad, nearly still support. This middle will develop a regular plucked-bass tread. Its continuity comes from the retained tonal centre, not from repeating the opening tune.
transitions.evidence: Section boundary: Minor-key middle, 270 s. The report marks 4:30, with increased brightness and attack density; C♯ minor estimates follow at 4:35–4:45. The score-based work guide establishes the change from D♭ major to C♯ minor and the ensuing pizzicato-bass passage; the estimates only corroborate it. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

transitions.title: Minor gives way to quicker figures
transitions.how: The minor-key lament draws inward before the little scherzo-like episode changes both mode and motion. C♯ remains the centre, but E♯ restores its major third; short wind and string figures replace the preceding longer phrases and measured bass steps. The quicker surface is not yet the great orchestral climax. Dvořák first builds a lighter, articulated texture, then lets its repetitions gather weight. The shared tonic connects the contrasting characters without a modulation to a distant key.
transitions.evidence: Section boundary: Quicker episode, 465 s. Attacks rise from 0.2/s at 7:35–7:40 to 4.6/s at 7:45, with relative level growing afterwards. The work guide identifies a quasi-scherzo in C♯ major after the minor section. The tempo character comes from the score, not the onset-tempo estimate. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

transitions.title: The dance admits remembered themes
transitions.how: The quicker episode grows into a confrontation rather than closing as an independent miniature. Increasing orchestral weight brings back material from the symphony’s first movement alongside the Largo’s own theme. Brass projection and the expanded bass foundation replace the preceding light exchanges, while the major-key ease gives way to minor colouring. The join works by accumulation: familiar ideas are made simultaneous, so the solitary song now belongs to a much larger argument. Listen for the broader thematic shapes through the busier surface.
transitions.evidence: Section boundary: Central crest, 490 s. The report marks 8:10 and its highest relative-level window there, after a sustained build from 7:45. The work guide identifies the combined Largo theme and first-movement main and closing themes. The report cannot isolate their entries, so the description covers the crest rather than a single attack. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

transitions.title: The orchestra releases the song
transitions.how: The climax loses force and orchestral mass before the song returns in D♭ major. The minor-coloured central region gives way to F♮, the major third of the recovered tonic; the bass no longer needs to propel a confrontation between themes. The cor anglais regains a quiet melodic role, and the later continuation reduces the strings towards chamber scale. Dvořák restores the tune’s dotted rhythm and narrow pitch collection but makes its exposure after the tutti part of the return.
transitions.evidence: Section boundary: Song returns, 520 s. Relative level recedes from the 8:10 crest to 8:40, one of the strongest detected boundaries. The score establishes D♭ major and the reduced return; the provisional relation matches 520–547.5 s with the opening song. It does not time an individual cor anglais entrance.

transitions.title: The introduction becomes a closing frame
transitions.how: The returning song has been thinned and broken into quieter phrases. Dvořák then replaces the melodic foreground with the introduction’s measured wind-chord writing. Chromatic inner movement again makes successive block chords feel connected, while the bass gives each harmony a separate footing. This time the chords do not introduce another song: they direct the remaining resonance towards D♭ major and the final low-string withdrawal. The movement closes by recalling its harmonic frame rather than repeating its melody at full strength.
transitions.evidence: Section boundary: Closing chords, 644 s. The report marks changes at 10:40 and 10:44; brightness is low through the ensuing chordal span, followed by the final retreat. The work guide documents the return of the introductory chords at the close; the description does not claim that every chord is repeated unchanged. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

source.title: Dvořák, Symphony No. 9, II. Largo, full score (Otakar Šourek edition)
source.locator: pp. 73–92, bars 1–127; the cor anglais song, minor middle, quicker episode, chamber-sized return and final wind frame are distinguished.

timeline.note: Clarinets, bassoons and brass move in block chords; timpani and muted strings support the arrival in D♭.
Cor anglais sings above muted strings; clarinet figures later move gently beneath the melody.
Wind phrases expand into a brief brass-supported swell before the string song resumes.
First violins take the melody before cor anglais recovers it; soft wind responses colour the string support.
Flutes and oboes move together in the minor-key middle above repeated inner-string chords.
Oboe and clarinet lines answer the violins; measured pizzicato lower strings give the lament its tread.
The minor passage draws inward; small wind figures remain distinct above the quieter strings.
A solo oboe figure grows into quicker woodwind exchanges; strings accumulate beneath their trills and runs.
Brass recalls first-movement ideas against the Largo material; winds and strings thicken above timpani rolls.
Cor anglais regains the song over quiet strings after the orchestral confrontation.
Muted strings reduce to two players per part, then exposed solos, with pauses between the phrases.
Bassoons, horns, trombones and tuba restore the chordal frame; strings briefly reconnect with its cadence.
The last wind chord releases the strings; divided double basses complete the quiet withdrawal.

composer.background:
Dvořák was born in Nelahozeves, a village north of Prague, where his father kept an inn and worked as a butcher. He learnt violin locally and acquired further musical training at Zlonice before attending the Prague Organ School in 1857–59. He earned his living in ensembles, including the orchestra of Prague’s Provisional Theatre from 1862 to 1871, playing viola under conductors who included Smetana. Opera taught him how a middle part supports singers, how repeated figures sustain a scene and how instrumental colour carries across a crowded theatre.

His early compositions were extensive and often ambitious: chamber music, symphonies and operatic projects accumulated before he had a dependable publisher. Wagner’s influence is audible in the scale and harmonic movement of some of these works. In 1873 he married Anna Čermáková. Teaching and an organist’s post helped support the household while applications for an Austrian state stipend brought his scores to influential readers. The award first received in 1875 brought both honour and money at a point when publication and commissions remained uncertain.
composer.epithet: A theatre violist who made dance accents, remembered songs and classical development work inside the same movement.
